archetype.name: Playoff Team (puck-possession)
archetype.definition: A Florida side that controls territory and suppresses shots well enough to sit comfortably in the playoff picture, without the chance-quality edge or the elite goaltending of its Cup-run years.

report.headline: Florida is back to driving play; the finish just hasn't caught up yet
report.take:
Last season looked like the end of something. Florida went 40-38-4, ranked 24th on the site, allowed goals at the 28th-best rate and got -8.8 goals saved above expected from its goalies. Twenty-two games into 2026-27, it is 12-7-3 and sixth on the Teams tab, on pace for 101 standings points. That is a real recovery. It is also not yet the 2023-24 team that ranked second and lifted the Cup.

The engine is possession and suppression. Florida takes 54% of the 5-on-5 shot attempts, fourth in the league. It fires 29.2 shots a game, seventh, and allows only 24.8, sixth. The penalty kill runs at 85.9%, fourth and well above the league's 77.4%. The power play, at 24.7%, is comfortably above average too. Up front the Tkachuk brothers carry it. Matthew has 30 points, 25 of them assists, and Brady has 23 points on a team-high 79 shots. Seth Jones logs 24.54 minutes a night and has 23 points, 14 on the power play. The record isn't padded either: Pts vs Goal Diff is a neutral 0.2, so the standings reflect the goal margin.

What the numbers hide cuts both ways. The 5-on-5 PDO is 97.8, so even-strength shooting and saving have run cold. The all-situations shooting % of 10.9% sits below the league's 11.4%. Both point to more goals coming. The other side is the expected-goals share. At 50.5% it ranks only 17th, far behind the 54% attempt share, so Florida has the puck more than it gets dangerous looks with it. Sam Reinhart is the clearest case: 12 goals, but a .452 xGF %.

The last 10 games went 6-3-1, outscoring opponents by 0.58 goals a game more than the season rate, and the last five allowed just 2.4 a game. That trend is believable because it rests on shot suppression rather than a hot goalie. In a crowded Atlantic, where Florida is fifth by record, it should keep them on the right side of the cut line.

strengths.title: Owning the puck and the shot clock
strengths.body: Florida ranks fourth in shot-attempt share and is top-seven in both shots for and shots against per game. That is a structural, process-driven edge, the same profile its contending teams had in history, so it should hold. It is also why the goaltending doesn't need to steal games.

strengths.title: An elite penalty kill
strengths.body: An 85.9% kill ranks fourth and sits far above the league average. It is a major reason the defense ranks 10th by goals against after finishing 28th last year. Kills that high usually drift down somewhat, but the low shot volume Florida allows at even strength suggests the structure is sound.

strengths.title: Tkachuk-driven power play
strengths.body: Matthew Tkachuk has 16 PP points and Brady 13, with Jones adding 14 from the point, behind a 24.7% power play. Both Tkachuks sit inside the top 10 of the left-wing tab, so this is top-end talent rather than a lucky run.

concerns.title: Attempts without enough quality
concerns.body: A 54% attempt share but only a 50.5% expected-goals share means much of the territory turns into low-danger volume. Reinhart's .452 xGF % is the clearest example: he scores at the top of the lineup while his line gets out-chanced. Unless chance quality improves, the team's ceiling is a good playoff team rather than a favorite.

concerns.title: Two very different goalies
concerns.body: The starts are split almost evenly, but the results aren't. Jacob Markstrom has a .906 save % and 3.7 GSAx. Akira Schmid sits at .885 and -0.8. Team GSAx is positive only because of Markstrom, and last year's goaltending collapse shows how quickly that can turn.

concerns.title: Thin bottom of the blueline
concerns.body: Kulikov and Gudas rank 181st and 187th on the defense tab and are being out-chanced, at .427 and .452 xGF %. The B+ blueline grade leans on Jones and on Ekblad's .600 xGF %. Opponents' centers are also getting a larger share of the points against Florida than the league norm.

trend.note: A .500-ish October gave way to a 6-3-1 last 10 with a much better goal margin than the season rate. The last five allowed just 2.4 goals a game as the shot suppression began to show up on the scoreboard.

weekAhead.headline: Two home games: a shaky-looking juggernaut, then a leaky Buffalo
weekAhead.body:
Edmonton arrives 16-3-3 and third on the site, but its underlying numbers say its record is running ahead of its play. Its xGF % is 47.3% (24th) and its CF % 48% (22nd). It shoots a league-best 15.6% for a league-high 106.3 all-situations PDO, with 2.7 points beyond its goal differential. Florida's possession game is exactly what tests that. The catch is A- goaltending and a defense that holds forwards well under their expected output, especially centers.

Buffalo is the softer second half: 8-8-4, 22nd on the site, with D- goaltending, a 70.4% penalty kill (27th) and the league's lowest all-situations PDO. Its A- blueline and 53% CF % mean it won't be pushed around at 5-on-5, but Florida's power play should find room. Two home games against this pair is a chance to bank three or four points.

keyMatchups.title: Tkachuk wingers versus Edmonton's weak spot
keyMatchups.body: Edmonton holds centers well under expectation (sixth), yet wingers take a larger share of the points scored against it than the league norm. That points the attack toward the Tkachuks on the flanks rather than Reinhart down the middle.

keyMatchups.title: Edmonton's finishing against Florida's suppression
keyMatchups.body: Edmonton generates only 25.3 shots a game (28th) and lives on a 15.6% shooting rate. If Florida keeps the shot count low, as it has all year, Edmonton needs that unsustainable finishing to hold for one more night.

keyMatchups.title: Florida power play versus Buffalo kill
keyMatchups.body: Buffalo kills only 70.4% of penalties and is the league's worst at limiting centers relative to their averages. Its goalies sit at an .873 save %. Reinhart, with 10 PP points, and Verhaeghe should get chances to convert.

weekAhead.watch: Whether Markstrom starts against Edmonton. The gap between the two goalies is the biggest variable in a game against the league's hottest finishers.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation is sustainable: top-five shot suppression, a top-five attempt share and a strong kill, with a neutral close-game record that hasn't flattered the standings. The 5-on-5 PDO of 97.8 and below-average shooting should drift upward, which argues for a slightly better goal margin from here. The penalty kill will likely cool from 85.9%, which roughly offsets that. The 101-point pace looks about right, with a reasonable range around it.

What separates a mid-seed from a division contender is chance quality and goaltending. The expected-goals share needs to move toward the attempt share. Markstrom also needs to keep carrying a heavier share of starts, because Schmid's numbers resemble last season's problems. In an Atlantic where five teams are bunched near the top, Florida projects as a playoff team, most likely as a wild card or the third seed rather than the division winner.
swingFactors: Markstrom's share of starts and form
